questions.q: What is the condition for a system of linear equations \(AX = B\) to have a unique solution using the matrix method?
questions.a: The condition is \(|A| \neq 0\) (i.e., the coefficient matrix \(A\) must be non-singular). A wrong answer such as "\(|A| = 0\)" or "\(A\) is singular" reveals the student confuses the condition for existence of inverse with the condition for unique solution. This is a critical conceptual error because if \(|A| = 0\), \(A^{-1}\) does not exist and the matrix method fails.

questions.q: A student writes the system \(3x - 2y = 7, \; 5x + 4y = 1\) as \(AX = B\) with \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\\5 & 4\end{bmatrix}\), \(X = \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}7\\1\end{bmatrix}\). They compute \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{22}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2\\-5 & 3\end{bmatrix}\) and then \(X = A^{-1}B\). They get \(x = \frac{15}{11}, y = \frac{-16}{11}\). Is their \(A^{-1}\) correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: The adjoint of \(A\) should be \(\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2\\-5 & 3\end{bmatrix}\)? Let's check: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\\5 & 4\end{bmatrix}\), cofactors: \(A_{11}=4, A_{12}=-5, A_{21}=2, A_{22}=3\). So \(\text{adj } A = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 2\\-5 & 3\end{bmatrix}^T = \begin{bmatrix}4 & -5\\2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\). The student forgot to transpose the cofactor matrix. Their \(A^{-1}\) is wrong. A wrong answer that says "yes it's correct" reveals the student does not understand that adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, a very common error in Class 12.

questions.q:
Solve the system using the matrix method:
\(x + 2y = 5\)
\(3x - y = 4\)
Show all steps including finding \(A^{-1}\).
questions.a:
Step 1: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\3 & -1\end{bmatrix}, X = \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}, B = \begin{bmatrix}5\\4\end{bmatrix}\).
Step 2: \(|A| = (1)(-1) - (2)(3) = -1 - 6 = -7 \neq 0\).
Step 3: Cofactors: \(A_{11} = -1, A_{12} = -3, A_{21} = -2, A_{22} = 1\). \(\text{adj } A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2\\-3 & 1\end{bmatrix}^T = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3\\-2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\).
Step 4: \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{-7}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3\\-2 & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1/7 & 3/7\\2/7 & -1/7\end{bmatrix}\).
Step 5: \(X = A^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix}1/7 & 3/7\\2/7 & -1/7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5\\4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}(5+12)/7\\ (10-4)/7\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}17/7\\ 6/7\end{bmatrix}\).
So \(x = 17/7, y = 6/7\). A wrong answer often comes from sign errors in cofactors or forgetting to divide by \(|A|\). If a student gets \(x=1, y=2\) they likely solved by substitution and didn't use the matrix method correctly.

questions.q: Compare the matrix method and Cramer's rule for solving a 3×3 system. Which method is more efficient when you only need the value of one variable (say \(z\))? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Cramer's rule is more efficient when only one variable is needed because you only compute two determinants: \(|A|\) and the determinant with the constant column replacing the \(z\)-column. The matrix method requires computing the full inverse (all 9 cofactors, adjoint, division by \(|A|\)) and then multiplying by \(B\), which is more work. A wrong answer claiming matrix method is faster reveals the student doesn't understand the computational load of finding the inverse versus a single determinant replacement. This is a frequent JEE trap where they ask "find \(z\) only" to test method selection.

questions.q: A student solves \(AX = B\) with \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3\\0 & 1 & 4\\5 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}\) and finds \(|A| = 0\). They then compute \((\text{adj } A)B\) and get a non-zero matrix. They conclude the system has infinitely many solutions. Is this conclusion correct? Explain.
questions.a: No, the conclusion is incorrect. If \(|A| = 0\) and \((\text{adj } A)B \neq O\), the system is **inconsistent** (no solution). Infinitely many solutions occur only when \(|A| = 0\) **and** \((\text{adj } A)B = O\). The student confused the two subcases. This is a classic board exam error: mixing up the conditions for inconsistency vs. infinite solutions. A wrong answer here costs full marks in a 4-mark question.

questions.q: Create a real-life problem (Indian context) that leads to a system of three linear equations in three variables. The system must have a unique solution. Write the problem, form the matrix equation, and solve it using the matrix method. Ensure the numbers are realistic (e.g., prices in rupees, quantities in kg).
questions.a:
Example problem: "A fruit vendor sells apples, bananas, and oranges. 2 kg apples, 1 kg bananas, and 3 kg oranges cost ₹210. 1 kg apples, 2 kg bananas, and 1 kg oranges cost ₹130. 3 kg apples, 1 kg bananas, and 2 kg oranges cost ₹220. Find the cost per kg of each fruit."
Matrix: \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3\\1 & 2 & 1\\3 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}, B = \begin{bmatrix}210\\130\\220\end{bmatrix}\).
\(|A| = 2(4-1) -1(2-3) +3(1-6) = 6 +1 -15 = -8 \neq 0\).
Cofactors and adjoint computed correctly yield \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{-8}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -5\\1 & -5 & 1\\-5 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\).
\(X = A^{-1}B = \frac{1}{-8}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -5\\1 & -5 & 1\\-5 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}210\\130\\220\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{-8}\begin{bmatrix}630+130-1100\\ 210-650+220\\ -1050+130+660\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{-8}\begin{bmatrix}-340\\ -220\\ -260\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}42.5\\ 27.5\\ 32.5\end{bmatrix}\).
Costs: apple ₹42.5/kg, banana ₹27.5/kg, orange ₹32.5/kg. A poor answer would use trivial numbers (like all 1s) or fail to set up the matrix correctly, showing inability to translate words to mathematics.
